newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil orange growers want benefits of tax change.
newsitem.headline: Brazil orange growers want benefits of tax change.

text.p: Brazil orange producers are campaigning to be reimbursed by juice processors after the scrapping of a state export tax which they say has always been deducted from prices paid to growers, an official said.
"Processors have always said in the past that if the tax was lifted, producers would benefit," said Leonardo Kossoy, president of the Sao Paulo Association of Citrus Growers.
"Now, however, they are saying that this was only if the tax was abolished for orange juice but because the recent exemption was general, it is different," he added.
The tax in question was lifted in mid-September this year for primary and semi-manufactured goods which previously carried a charge of up to 13 percent.
Under a master contract used in other years by processors and producers, the tax was deducted, along with other costs, from the price paid to growers.
"The contract also said that if any new tax was levied it would be the responsibility of the producer," Kossoy said.
This year however producers and processors are using individual contracts after an anti-trust commission ruled in favor of growers who had claimed processors were operating a buyers' cartel.
A small percentage of growers still included the tax clause in their new contracts, giving them a judicial basis to make a claim against sales from mid-September, Kossoy said.
However, most growers have no legal recourse and so growers' associations are trying to lobby on the political level.
One supporter is Francisco Graziano, recently apponted Agriculture Secretary of Sao Paulo state, who has often heard processors promise to pass over the benefits of any tax exemption, Kossoy said.
Processors have recently started to pay higher prices but this is mainly in reaction to smaller fruit size which is reducing the percentage of the crop which can be used by the industry, he added.
The Brazilian Association of Citrus Exporters (Abecitrus) has estimated the 1996/97 crop at 352 million 40.8-kg boxes, virtually unchanged from last year.

However around 10 percent of this is not suitable for use by processors because the oranges are too small, a direct result of growers having insufficient funds to buy fertilizers and other necessary inputs, Kossoy said.
This fruit cannot even be sold to the domestic market as "people don't want to buy fruit that looks like a hen's egg so it will just be lost," he added.

Given that supply for processing is now expected to be tighter than earlier forecast, prices started to edge up in September and particularly in October, with the industry now paying $3 a box for Pera Rio variety on trucks at the orchard.
This is better than the $1.80 a box paid for Hamlin oranges at the factory in July, although Pera Rio would normally command higher prices, Kossoy said.
Very few farmers however will have been able to wait to sell their product until this month, with most probably settling for around $2 a box, he added.
Abecitrus officials were not immediately available for comment.
